passage:
I'm Chinmay, and in my first month at the hostel in Manipal I said yes to everything. Instant noodles on the terrace at midnight, yes. A trip to the beach at six in the morning, yes. A quiz club I had no interest in, also yes. My room felt too quiet otherwise.
Thomas was in the room opposite, from Kottayam. On the fourth night we both admitted we'd cried after our parents left. By the second week we were sharing a toothpaste tube and finishing each other's jokes, and I told Amma on the phone that I'd found my best friend.
Looking back, I'm a little embarrassed by how fast I said that. We'd known each other eleven days. The warmth was real, but a lot of it was two homesick boys holding on to the first person who understood. We're still friends. Just the ordinary, slower kind.

qa.q: What did Thomas and Chinmay admit on the fourth night?
qa.a: They both admitted they'd cried after their parents left.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay say yes to every invitation in the first month?
qa.a: Chinmay was lonely and the room felt too quiet otherwise, so every plan was a way not to be alone.

qa.q: What could Chinmay keep in mind during this open-door stage?
qa.a: Chinmay could enjoy the quick warmth while letting friendships grow at their own pace, instead of naming someone a best friend after eleven days.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt in those first weeks?
qa.a: Thomas was homesick too, so finding Chinmay across the corridor probably felt like relief and a safe person to hold on to.

grounding: Shows a lonely, eager first-year hostel student saying yes to everything and forming a quick, homesick closeness that felt stronger than it yet was.

passage:
Trainee batch note, week three. From the training coordinator.
Saurabh (from Patna, first job, first time living away from home) has joined every plan in the batch so far: the Friday biryani run, the Sunday fort trek, even the badminton group, though he told me he "can't really play". He is always the first to reply "I'm in" on the batch group.
He and Sonali, from Guwahati, seem to have become very close very quickly. I often see them in the cafeteria after nine, talking about home food and their mothers' phone calls. Last week Sonali said to me, laughing, "He's already like my brother."
It is lovely to see, and it is helping both of them settle. I have also noticed that Saurabh looks lost on evenings when no plan is on. I've paired him with a senior buddy for the next month and will mention the wellness sessions at our check-in.

qa.q: What does Saurabh reply on the batch group?
qa.a: Saurabh is always the first to reply 'I'm in' on the batch group.

qa.q: Why might Saurabh join every plan, even badminton?
qa.a: Saurabh is far from home for the first time and probably lonely; saying yes keeps away the empty evenings, which is when he looks lost.

qa.q: What did the coordinator do well to support Saurabh at this stage?
qa.a: The coordinator noticed the pattern without judging it, paired Saurabh with a senior buddy and planned to mention the wellness sessions, giving steadier support than one fast friendship.

qa.q: How might Sonali see the closeness with Saurabh?
qa.a: Sonali seems to enjoy it and already calls him like a brother, because sharing homesickness makes the bond feel strong very fast.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult in a first-job city saying yes to every invitation, with shared homesickness creating quick closeness.

Wanjiru had been in Glasgow for nine days and had said yes to everything.

Yes to the pub quiz with people from her corridor. Yes to the midnight walk to see the river. Yes to Sofia from the room next door, who knocked on day two holding a pot of lentil soup and said, "I made too much, and I miss my mother's cooking."

By the end of the first week they had eaten together six times. They sat on Sofia's floor until two in the morning, trading homesick stories: Sofia's grandmother's garden in Porto, the smell of rain on Wanjiru's street in Nairobi.

"I feel like I've known you for years," Sofia said on Friday.

Wanjiru felt the same, and a small part of her wondered how that could be true after nine days. She pushed the thought away and said yes to Saturday's trip to the coast.

qa.q: What did Sofia bring when she first knocked on Wanjiru's door?
qa.a: A pot of lentil soup.

qa.q: What is Wanjiru feeling when a small part of her wonders how it can be true after nine days?
qa.a: She feels happy and close to Sofia but also slightly unsure, sensing the closeness may be stronger than it has had time to become.

qa.q: What would you advise Wanjiru as she keeps saying yes to everything?
qa.a: Enjoy the new friendships, but let them grow at their own pace and keep a little time for rest, so the early closeness can be tested over time.

qa.q: How does Sofia see their friendship after a week?
qa.a: She feels as if she has known Wanjiru for years, likely because shared homesickness makes her feel understood and less alone.

grounding: New to Glasgow, lonely Wanjiru says yes to every invitation, and shared meals and homesick late-night talks with Sofia create a quick closeness that may feel stronger than it is.

passage:
The warden of the women's hostel in Pune had warned the first-years: "You will make best friends in a week. Some of them will last."

Payal laughed at that. Then Gargi moved in across the corridor.

On the first night the power went out, and they sat in the corridor with phone torches, eating Gargi's mother's laddoos. On the second night they walked to the chai stall at eleven. By Thursday they knew each other's childhood fears, favourite songs, and why Gargi's father didn't call.

Payal had never talked like this with anyone. Back home she had been the quiet one.

"It's funny," Gargi said, lying on Payal's floor. "I feel like you know me better than my school friends."

Payal felt warm all over. Somewhere at the back of her mind, the warden's words came back: some of them will last.

qa.q: What did they eat on the first night when the power went out?
qa.a: Gargi's mother's laddoos.

qa.q: How does Payal feel when Gargi says Payal knows her better than her school friends?
qa.a: Payal feels warm and happy, even thrilled, because back home she had been the quiet one; but the warden's words bring a small note of doubt.

qa.q: How could the hostel warden support first-years like Payal and Gargi?
qa.a: The warden could keep offering shared activities and gently remind students that new closeness is real but still growing, so no one feels crushed if it changes.

qa.q: What might the warden's warning mean to Gargi, if she heard it?
qa.a: She might feel a little defensive, wanting to believe this friendship is different, but it could also help her pace it.

grounding: In a Pune hostel, Payal and Gargi form fast intimacy through shared food, late walks and homesick confessions, a closeness that feels stronger than it yet is.

passage:
Hi Amma,

Week three in Bengaluru. Before you worry: I'm eating properly.

I have to tell you, I've made friends already. Remember how I thought I'd be alone here? A girl called Ira from my team invited me for lunch on day one and I said yes. Then dinner. Then a Saturday trip to the lake with five people I'd met twice.

I say yes to everything. The PG room is too quiet otherwise.

Ira and I stay up talking on the terrace till one. She misses her dog, I miss your rasam. We laugh about it. It feels like we've been friends for years, which is strange, because it's been nineteen days.

Sometimes I wonder if I'm going too fast. But it's better than eating alone.

Send the rasam powder with Mama's parcel, please.

Jeevan

qa.q: Where do Ira and Jeevan stay up talking till one?
qa.a: On the terrace.

qa.q: Why does Jeevan say yes to everything?
qa.a: Jeevan feels lonely in the quiet PG room and is eager for company, so every invitation feels better than eating alone.

qa.q: What could Jeevan try so the new friendships grow well?
qa.a: Keep enjoying them but let them deepen over time, maybe keeping a few quieter evenings, so the quick closeness has time to become real.

qa.q: How might Amma feel reading this email?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that Jeevan has friends, and a little wistful at being missed through the rasam.

grounding: Jeevan's email to Amma shows a lonely newcomer in a first job city saying yes to every invitation and feeling quick intimacy through homesick talks.

So, the first month in the Delhi hostel? I'm Yamini, and I said yes to everything. Everything.

Instant noodles at 2 a.m. in Room 14? Yes. Chai walk to the gate at midnight? Yes. Someone's cousin's birthday in Lajpat Nagar? Absolutely yes.

I was so lonely those first nights that any open door felt like a lifeline. And Sudha, from Room 16, she was the same. We'd sit on her floor talking about how much we missed home, her mother's rasam, my brother's awful jokes. By week three we were calling each other "sister."

Looking back, it was real, but it was also fast. We knew each other's childhood fears before we knew each other's middle names. It felt like we'd been friends for years. It had been nineteen days.

qa.q: Which room was Sudha in?
qa.a: Sudha was in Room 16.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling in those first nights at the hostel?
qa.a: Yamini felt lonely and homesick, so every open door and invitation felt like a lifeline.

qa.q: What could Yamini keep in mind as these quick friendships grow?
qa.a: That early closeness can feel stronger than it is yet, so it helps to let trust build over time while enjoying it.

qa.q: How might Sudha have felt about their quick bond?
qa.a: Sudha seemed equally lonely and glad of the company, finding comfort in sharing homesickness.

grounding: A spoken account shows a lonely young adult saying yes to every hostel invitation, with shared homesickness creating quick intimacy.
